name: Amazonas
summary_text: Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis following the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court, in the ADO 26 and MI 4733 proceedings, held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 puts the term at one to five years and confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.  No third-gender marker is available nationally, but civil registries have recorded non-binary or unspecified entries since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of a registry entry to a neutral gender as precedent.  Arrest and imprisonment carry a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the placement is fixed by a reasoned decision taken after the person has been consulted about their preference, and the declared preference is recorded and may be changed later. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  The protective text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report states that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, notwithstanding the constitutional and criminal provisions.  The expatriate guide records uneven enforcement as a feature of the current regime: major cities are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. The sources assembled for this record contain no Amazonas-specific evidence identifying which condition holds in which part of the state.

name: Bahia
summary_text: Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil and stands under the national framework described above: the federal constitutional and criminal prohibitions on SOGI discrimination, the 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, equal age of consent, same-sex marriage and spousal-visa equality, and National Council of Justice Resolution 348/366 governing the placement of LGBTI detainees all extend to Bahia and to its prison system.  Bahia records one of the country's highest burdens of trans and travesti killings. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only the states recording 8; on the same national reckoning, which counts 1,261 killings across Brazil from 2017 to 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo at 151 and Ceará at 107. Valor Internacional recorded the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, placing Bahia behind the Ceará and Minas Gerais pair.  The figure is persistent rather than a single-year outlier. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the Brazilian states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year, putting Bahia in the top band of consecutive annual dossiers.  Individual cases show how the violence is charged and processed. On the weekend of 6–7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of Bahia. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station himself, confessed, and claimed self-defence; he was released. The Civil Police confirmed that the case is being investigated as a feminicide, and the state police framed the killing as gender-based, so the killing of a trans woman in Bahia was classified as gender-based violence while the accused was initially set free.  For a trans visitor, the practical exposure is the violence risk and its investigative handling rather than any entry, document or visa rule: the national framework applies Bahia's entry and family-law treatment on the same footing as for anyone else, and no Bahia-specific rule governing where trans detainees are held was located in the sources reviewed.
